WHO Mortality Database: data harmonisation for the premature mortality project

2026-10-23

About this page

This page documents how the WHO Mortality Database was harmonised and cleaned for the project Premature mortality in successive birth cohorts across world regions: the data used and the rules that select them (Section 1), then, step by step, the raw files read, the countries kept, ages, causes across ICD revisions, coding changes, ill-defined causes, gaps, peaks, population, and how countries were pooled into areas (Section 1.1). It is Section 1 of the project report (code/08_report.Rmd, rendered by code/08_render.R), built from the same sources, code/08_data.Rmd and code/08_who_processing.Rmd, so the two give the same text and numbers; only the links, the notes on them and the layout of the Code: lines differ. Every number is computed from the output files of the project when the page is rendered (code/16_docs.R).

The report itself is not published online, as its results are unpublished. Section, table and figure numbers are those of the report, and its other parts are cited as in the report, so that the two documents stay identical: Sections 2-8 and the figures other than D1 are in the report only. The analyses of the report are cited as Result 1 (cohort SDG 3.4 and the period-cohort gap, report Section 2), Result 2 (leading premature cause by cohort, report Section 3) and Result 3 (tobacco cohort lag, report Section 4); Module B is one of the replicated European analyses (premature-death shares by generation, report Section 5.1).

Links. The Code: lines that end each part of Section 1.1 and the code map (Table 1.8) point to the R code that does each step. For the scripts of the data build (code/functions_pm.R, code/01_areas.R, code/02_cause_groups.R, code/03_who_deaths.R and code/04_area_series.R), shown in full in the appendix, the line numbers open the code on this page with those lines highlighted; for the page’s own sources they open GitHub. File names link to the files of the public repository (filhoalm/premature-mortality-cohorts), which holds this first component of the project: the code of the data harmonisation and this page (docs/published.csv). Data, outputs and the scripts of the analyses are not published yet and are named without a link. The appendix also describes the columns of the two dictionaries that drive the build.

Data and status. Deaths and population: WHO Mortality Database (February 2026 release), with population completed from the UN World Population Prospects; the raw files are not redistributed. Work in progress: the numbers may change; please contact the author before citing or reusing them. Licence (LICENSE, to be confirmed): code MIT License, data outputs Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0); check the WHO Mortality Database terms of use before sharing derived data.

1 Data

Source. WHO Mortality Database, February 2026 release (raw files downloaded from cdn.who.int on 10 October 2026, Eu40_APC NOTES item 2): deaths by country, year, sex, age group and cause for ICD-7 to ICD-10, and WHO population (mort_pop), read without modification. Cause groups and their ICD-7 to ICD-10 codes are in data/dict/who_cause_groups.csv; NCD4 = cancer (C00-C97) + cardiovascular diseases (I00-I99) + diabetes (E10-E14) + chronic respiratory diseases (J30-J98). Person-years are the WHO population where it exists, completed by the population of the UN World Population Prospects (revision to be confirmed), estican data/UNDP/pop_UN.rds of 2 June 2026 (as used for GLOBOCAN 2024; read-only), calibrated to WHO by sex and age; see Population below.

Areas and countries. The 227 WHO country codes are mapped to ISO3 and to UN M49 numeric codes and names of the country, region, sub-region and intermediate region (data/dict/areas.csv; historical M49 codes for former entities); 136 are eligible (former entities, parts of countries, overlapping codes, codes without national data and countries rated Low by the WHO data-quality assessment are excluded). The data hold 6,669 country-years with deaths (161 codes, 1950-2024). The area- and country-level outputs carry the UN M49 codes next to the names (region_code, area_code; m49_code for countries), except who_deaths.rds, who_checks.rds and list_transitions.csv (WHO code only), respiratory_checks.csv (WHO code and ISO3) and profiles.csv (area_code only); data/dict/areas.csv links the WHO code to ISO3 and the M49 codes (NOTES item 87).

WHO data-quality assessment. The WHO assessment of the mortality data (estican data/WHO_mortality_data_quality.csv, read-only; NOTES item 85) rates each country by usability = completeness of death registration x (1 - the share of ill-defined or non-specific causes): 98 codes are rated: 60 High, 25 Medium and 13 Low. The 13 countries rated Low are not eligible: Andorra, Bahrain, Bulgaria, Egypt, El Salvador, Iraq, Lebanon, Malaysia, Maldives, Morocco, Oman, Peru and Qatar. Of the 53 area countries, 36 are rated High, 11 are rated Medium and 6 are not rated (Table 1.3). The rating is one recent assessment applied to every year, so the year-level ill-defined rule below is kept.

Population. Person-years are the WHO population (mort_pop, ages harmonised as the deaths, gaps of 1-3 years interpolated) where it exists. Every other cell (country, year, sex and age) of a country-year with deaths takes the UN WPP population times the WHO/WPP ratio of that sex and age, averaged over the 3 nearest WHO years on each side, held beyond the first or last WHO year and interpolated between two seams (‘WPP calibrated’), so that the series follows the WHO level and keeps the territory covered by the WHO deaths; countries without any WHO population take WPP as published (‘WPP’; NOTES item 84). Table 1.1 gives the source at ages 30-69. At the seams, the calibration ratio of the cells at 30-69 lies between 0.243 and 2.064 (median 0.997); 868 of 2,930 cells lie outside 0.9-1.1, 142 of 816 in the countries of the areas (output/data_build/population_seams.csv). The 3-year mean ratio, not the ratio of the WHO year next to the seam, is carried across the seam, so the series steps there by the deviation of that WHO year from the mean: with step = calibrated/WPP in the WPP year over WHO/WPP in the adjacent WHO year, minus 1 (ages 30-69, both sexes), |step| exceeds 2% at 5 of the 28 seams inside the area windows (Guatemala +4.2% (WHO 1984, WPP 1985), Costa Rica -3.6% (WHO 2019, WPP 2020), Philippines +3.3% (WHO 2004, WPP 2003), Puerto Rico -3.2% (WHO 1992, WPP 1993) and Philippines -2.8% (WHO 1994, WPP 1993)) and is at most 2.0% at the others.

Usability rule (Results 1-2). A country-year is usable when person-years and the deaths of every needed cause group are available at every age 30-69 for both sexes, the codes of the WHO List add up to the all-cause code, and ill-defined causes are at most 20% of deaths at 30-69. 5,125 of 6,669 country-years are usable, in 148 countries (Table 1.2). COPD is not part of the rule; the years where it is isolable are flagged (copd_ok) and used in Result 3 only.

Windows. A country’s usable series is its longest run of consecutive usable years, and the 96 eligible countries with at least 20 usable years are candidates. Each area is a UN M49 sub-region: among the windows of at least 25 years (or of the longest usable run of the candidates where that is shorter: Southern Asia, 22 years), the window and the candidates covering all of it with the largest person-years at 30-69; deaths and person-years are summed over these countries. 13 areas with 53 countries result (Table 1.3, Figure D1). Because the rule maximises person-years, a large country can shorten a window: leaving out one country would lengthen it by at least 10 years in Sub-Saharan Africa (without ZAF: MUS 1969-2024, 0.05 of the person-years), Eastern Asia (without KOR: HKG JPN 1969-2023, 0.98 of the person-years), South-eastern Asia (without PHL: SGP 1969-2022, 0.09 of the person-years) and Western Europe (without DEU: AUT BEL CHE FRA NLD 1969-2022, 0.84 of the person-years). The windows cover 2015 in 12 areas, not in Western Asia (ends 2007); the only alternative covering it is Western Asia ARM ISR KWT 1993-2023 (0.84 of the person-years), not used. Eastern Asia without Korea (HKG JPN 1969-2023, 0.98 of the person-years) starts 16 years earlier and is a supplementary area in Result 2.

Data caveats.

  • 304 country-years are interpolated across gaps of 1-3 years and 22 are composites (Germany before 1990 = FRG + GDR; United Kingdom 2000 = its parts); both count as usable and are marked in D1, as are the years with WPP person-years.
  • Territory changes inside windows: MUS 2018 (person-years 30-69 vs 2017: country +3.3%, area +4.2%); GEO 1994 (person-years 30-69 vs 1992: country -9.0%, area +1.2%); MDA 1997 (person-years 30-69 vs 1996: country -16.2%, area -0.7%); RUS 1993 (person-years 30-69 vs 1992: country +0.1%, area +0.1%); RUS 2004 (person-years 30-69 vs 2003: country +0.6%, area +0.5%); UKR 2014 (person-years 30-69 vs 2012: country -3.2%, area +0.7%). Deaths and population refer to the same territory, so rates stay consistent; none of these changes falls in WPP years.
  • Ill-defined causes are 0.5% (Australia and New Zealand) to 12.1% (Sub-Saharan Africa) of deaths at 30-69 over the windows and are not redistributed.
  • COPD (J40-J47) is isolable only in some WHO Lists (copd_ok years); where too few such years remain, the COPD lag is not assessable (Section 4).

1.1 How the WHO Mortality Database was processed

This section explains, step by step, what was done to the WHO data before any analysis, what was deliberately left as reported, and why. Each part starts with a short summary in plain words, followed by the exact rule and, where relevant, what was not done, and ends with links to the R code that does the step and to the files that hold the details. File names open the files in the GitHub repository (main branch), for readers with access to it. The line numbers of the data-build scripts open their code in the appendix of this page, the others the script on GitHub at those lines; they are read from the scripts each time this page is rendered. The .rds files (R data, read with readRDS()) are not in the repository (rebuilt by the scripts); their columns are described in data/derived/dictionary.csv.

Terms used here.

  • ICD: International Classification of Diseases, revisions 7 to 10.
  • List: a WHO cause list, the set of codes a country used in a year, for example 104 = ICD-10 at four characters (Table 1.5).
  • NCD4: cancer, cardiovascular diseases, diabetes and chronic respiratory diseases, the four groups of SDG target 3.4.
  • F1: the period SDG 3.4 indicator, the probability of dying from NCD4 between 30 and 70 at the death rates of one calendar year (Figure F1, Section 2).
  • Usable year: a country-year that passes the usability rule: every needed cause group can be separated at every age 30-69, the population is known, WHO’s chapter totals add up to its all-cause total, and ill-defined causes are at most 20% of deaths at 30-69.
  • Window: the years over which an area is followed, with the same countries in every year.
  • Composite: a series built by adding up its parts (Germany 1969-1989 and United Kingdom 2000).
  • WPP calibrated: UN World Population Prospects population, scaled to the WHO population by sex and age.
  • Study sub-project (Study/): the repetition of Bray et al. 2021 (premature NCD deaths, 2000-2019) for the same areas; its sensitivity analysis F8 redistributes ill-defined deaths.
  • Eu40_APC: the sister project on European generations, whose raw WHO files and methods are reused here. It is a separate project: its files, the raw WHO files among them, are not in this repository; the WHO files can be downloaded from the WHO Mortality Database.

In brief

  • The raw data. The WHO Mortality Database (February 2026 release) gives the deaths registered in each country by year, sex, age group and cause, coded with ICD-7 to ICD-10 in 12 WHO cause lists, together with WHO population figures. The raw files were only read, never edited: every step below is done in R and writes new files.
  • What was changed. Ages were put into the same 18 five-year groups, deaths of unknown age were shared out over the ages pro rata within each cause group, and gaps of 1-3 years were filled with a straight line. Two series were completed from their parts (Germany 1969-1989 and United Kingdom 2000), and missing population was taken from the UN World Population Prospects (WPP), adjusted to the WHO level.
  • What was not changed: ill-defined causes. Deaths certified only with a symptom or an unknown cause (ICD-10 R00-R99 and the matching codes of earlier revisions) stay a group of their own and were not shared out among the other causes, pro rata or otherwise; years where they exceed 20% of deaths at 30-69 are not used. A pro-rata redistribution was tested only in a sensitivity analysis of the Study sub-project (F8), for the 2000-2019 change of the period NCD4 indicator (largest effect in Southern Asia: -8.0% as certified, -18.1% redistributed); its effect on Results 1-3 was not computed (Table 1.6).
  • Other things left as reported. Deaths of unknown sex were dropped, age groups merged by a country (for example 75 and over) were left missing, and the WHO population was used as published. Changes of WHO cause list were flagged, not corrected.
  • What was kept. Only national data, one code per territory and no country rated Low by WHO; a year is used only if every needed cause group can be separated at 30-69, the population is known, WHO’s chapter totals add up to its all-cause total and ill-defined causes are at most 20%. Each area sums a fixed set of countries over a fixed window, each country contributing its longest unbroken run of such years (Table 1.4).
  • Gaps. Only runs of 1-3 missing years were filled; longer gaps break a country’s series. Filled years are 55 of the 2,133 country-years in the area windows (1.4% of the person-years at 30-69).
  • Peaks. No year was removed, smoothed or corrected because of a peak. All 85 year-to-year changes of at least 1 percentage point in F1 (the period SDG 3.4 indicator: the probability of dying from NCD4 between 30 and 70 at one calendar year’s death rates) are in Table 1.7 with a verdict: some are real events (crises, a disaster, COVID-19), some come from the data (a change of cause list, filled years, a step in the population), and some are not explained.
  • Where to check. Each part below ends with links to the R code, Table 1.8 maps every step to its code, and the decisions are numbered in NOTES.md.

From the WHO files to the area series. Table 1.4 follows the country-years through the build. The build applies the usability rule to every code and eligibility afterwards; the counts below do not depend on the order. Table 1.2 counts the usable years of all codes, eligible or not (5,125); here only eligible codes are counted, from ‘Eligible codes’ on.

Raw files

In plain words. Everything starts from the raw files of the WHO Mortality Database. They were downloaded once for the sister project Eu40_APC and are kept there in a read-only folder. There is one file of deaths per ICD revision (ICD-10 in several parts), two Excel workbooks for recent years of Germany and Norway, the population file, the list of country codes and WHO’s notes. Only national rows are used: rows for a region, a city or a population group are skipped.

Exact rule.

  • Source: WHO Mortality Database, February 2026 release (raw files downloaded from cdn.who.int on 10 October 2026, Eu40_APC NOTES item 2). Deaths: 9 files (MortIcd7, Morticd8, Morticd9, Morticd10_part1, Morticd10_part2, Morticd10_part3, Morticd10_part4, Morticd10_part5 and Morticd10_part6) and the workbooks Germany.xlsx and Norway.xlsx; population mort_pop, codes mort_country_codes and notes mort_notes, all in Eu40_APC/data/who_mortality/raw/. The documentation PDF (raw/mort_documentation/) is cited by page in the cause dictionary. mort_availability is not read: the years come from the rows themselves (NOTES items 2 and 32).
  • National rows are those with Admin1 and SubDiv blank. The national extract is cached and rebuilt whenever a raw file changes.
  • The Norway workbook (2017-2024) merges ages 0-14, which are left missing; ages 30-69 are complete, so these years are used. The Germany workbook (2021-2022) suppresses small cells, so only all-cause deaths are taken from it and these years are not usable (NOTES items 16-17).

Code:

  • code/functions_pm.R: raw files and release (who_raw, who_src, who_files, who_xl), lines 7-10
  • code/03_who_deaths.R: national rows only, keep(), lines 55-59; raw files read once and cached, lines 60-67
  • code/01_areas.R: years with national and regional rows per code, lines 53-62
  • Details: data/dict/areas.csv

Countries and data quality

In plain words. WHO uses its own country codes. Each code was given its ISO3 code and the UN M49 codes and names of its country, region and sub-region; the sub-region is the ‘area’ of this study. Some codes describe the same people twice: a country and its parts, or a former state and its successors. One code per territory is kept: the United Kingdom rather than its parts, unified Germany, and the successor states rather than the USSR, Czechoslovakia or Yugoslavia. Codes with regional data only are not used, and neither are countries rated Low in WHO’s own assessment of data quality. Two series were completed by adding up their parts. Changes of territory inside a series were documented but not adjusted, because the WHO deaths and the WHO population of a year cover the same territory.

Exact rule.

  • 227 WHO codes. ISO3 comes from the name (countrycode package), set by hand for former entities and parts of countries; the regions of 15 codes not in M49 were set by hand (NOTES items 4-5).
  • 136 codes are eligible and 91 are not (reasons in data/dict/areas.csv; NOTES item 6). 66 have no national rows: 61 have no rows at all, 4 have regional rows only (Bangladesh, China, Occupied Palestinian Territory and Pakistan) and 1 is a former entity without data (Sudan, Former). Of the codes with national rows, 25 are left out: 13 rated Low by WHO, 6 parts of countries and 6 former entities (Table 1.4). Regional rows, which 13 codes have, are never used.
  • WHO data-quality rating (above): of the eligible codes, 59 are rated High and 25 Medium, 47 are not in the WHO assessment and 5 are in it without a rating (Russian Federation, Seychelles, Solomon Islands, Turkmenistan and Ukraine; NOTES item 85).
  • Composites: deaths and person-years of the parts are added by year, sex, age and cause group (Germany 1969-1989 = 4100 + 4090 and United Kingdom 2000 = 4310 + 4320 + 4330, WHO codes; NOTES item 7).
  • Territory changes in 6 codes (Mauritius 2018, Japan 1972, Georgia 1994, Republic of Moldova 1997, Russian Federation 1993 and 2004 and Ukraine 2014) were not adjusted; their effect on the person-years inside the windows is in the Data caveats above (NOTES items 7 and 28).

Not done. The WHO rating is one recent assessment applied to every year: completeness of registration in earlier decades was not assessed or corrected, and no data were weighted by quality (NOTES item 85, Section 7).

Code:

  • code/01_areas.R: WHO codes to ISO3 and UN M49, lines 15-44; WHO data-quality rating, lines 48-50; years filled by composites, lines 70-71; eligibility (include, reason), lines 75-92; territory changes, lines 97-110
  • code/03_who_deaths.R: composites: parts added, lines 192-202
  • Details: data/dict/areas.csv

Ages

In plain words. Countries report deaths in different age layouts. Some give every five-year group up to 95 and over; others merge the old ages (for example 75 and over) or give no ages at all. All layouts were turned into the same 18 five-year groups, from 0-4 to 85 and over. When a country merged ages across these groups, the merged cells were left missing rather than split by assumption. Deaths of unknown age were shared out over the ages in proportion to the deaths of known age of the same cause group, in the same country, year and sex: each group keeps its age pattern and its number of deaths. Deaths of unknown sex were dropped.

Exact rule.

  • age18() adds the WHO age columns into 18 groups according to each row’s age format (the WHO variable Frmat; WHO documentation, Annex 1, PDF p.8). Formats 03 and 04 (75 and over merged), 05 (70 and over) and 06 (65 and over) leave the merged groups missing; 07 and 08 (ten-year groups) and 09 (no ages) leave every age missing; the Norway workbook leaves ages 0-14 missing.
  • Observed country-years by age format (6,344 in all):
    • every age (formats 00-02): 5,996;
    • ages from 70 or 75 on merged (formats 03-05): 81, of which 54 usable, since ages 30-69 are complete;
    • ages below 70 merged, or no ages (formats 06-09): 259, of which 0 usable;
    • the Norway workbook (ages 0-14 merged): 8, of which 8 usable.
  • In the area windows, old ages are merged in 5 country-years (CRI 1984; KOR 1995-1996; LKA 2015, 2019) and ages 0-14 in 6 (NOR 2017-2022). The area cells concerned are then missing. Later analyses fill them over 1-3 years (Eastern Asia 1995-1996, ages 75-84) or drop such years at a window end (Latin America and the Caribbean 1984; Southern Asia 2015-2019; Section 6, ‘Projections’).
  • Unknown age (WHO column 26, deaths of unknown age): at every age, the deaths of a group are multiplied by 1 + unknown/known, separately by country, year, sex and cause group; a group with deaths of unknown age only is left missing. All causes by age is then rebuilt as the sum of the six exclusive groups (below), so its age pattern follows the cause mix (NOTES item 16).
  • Unknown sex (WHO sex code 9): dropped, a very small number of deaths (NOTES item 16). The WHO population of unknown age is dropped as well (NOTES item 18).

Not done. Merged age groups were not split or modelled in the data build. The numbers of deaths of unknown age are not saved in any output file, so their size is not reported here (those of unknown sex are in NOTES item 16).

Code:

  • code/functions_pm.R: age18(): WHO age formats to 18 groups, merged groups missing, lines 24-31
  • code/03_who_deaths.R: unknown sex dropped, line 73; unknown age shared out within each group, line 112; all causes by age = sum of the exclusive groups, lines 120-122
  • Details: data/derived/who_deaths.rds (R data, not in the repository)

Causes across ICD revisions

In plain words. Between 1950 and 2024 countries coded deaths with the 7th to 10th ICD revisions and, within each, with condensed or detailed WHO cause lists (Table 1.5). One dictionary, data/dict/who_cause_groups.csv, says which codes of each list make up each cause group, with the page of the WHO documentation for every row. Six groups never overlap and add up to all causes: cancer, cardiovascular diseases, external causes, ill-defined causes, COVID-19 and ‘other’ (everything else). NCD4, the group of SDG 3.4, is cancer + cardiovascular diseases + diabetes + chronic respiratory diseases. When a list has no code for a group (for example ischaemic heart disease in ICD-7), the group is left missing, not estimated, and the year cannot be used for Results 1-2: no ICD-7 year is usable, so none is in the area windows.

Exact rule.

  • The dictionary has 278 rows for 12 Lists, each citing a page of the WHO documentation. Codes are matched exactly or on their first three characters, some rows subtract sub-items, and 32 rows are required sub-items: codes that must be reported in the country-year, or the group is missing (NOTES items 8-14).
  • 3 rows are comparability choices, each tested on the data (source column of the dictionary): cerebrovascular disease added to cardiovascular diseases (ICD-7 Lists 07A and 07B) and ICD-7 156 added to liver diseases (ICD-7 List 07A), so that these groups do not step at the move from ICD-7 to ICD-8. They decide which codes count in a group; no death counts were adjusted. As no ICD-7 year is usable, they do not affect the results.
  • ICD-10 codes (List 104): cancer C00-C97, cardiovascular diseases I00-I99, IHD I20-I25, stroke I60-I69, external causes V01-Y89, ill-defined causes R00-R99, COVID-19 U071, U072, U099, U109, diabetes E10-E14, COPD J40-J47, lung cancer C33-C34 and chronic respiratory diseases J30-J98; the codes of earlier revisions are in the dictionary.
  • ‘Other’ is all causes minus cancer, cardiovascular, external, ill-defined and COVID-19, and all causes by age is rebuilt as the sum of the six groups (Ages above), so the six add up to all causes by construction (13,252 of 13,252 country-year-sex cells, a check of the code). Two other checks can fail. First, the top-level codes of each List (its chapters) must add up to its all-cause code: this fails in 57 country-year-sex cells, in Germany (1977-1988 and 2021-2022); Germany, Former Democratic Republic (1977-1988); San Marino (2020-2022), where some codes are missing or suppressed in the WHO files. Second, ‘other’ must not be negative at any age in the raw counts, which would mean that the five other groups count some deaths twice: it never is. A country-year failing either check is not usable (‘codes do not add up’ in Tables 1.2 and 1.4). This is the first failing criterion in 24 country-years: Germany (1977-1988); Germany, Former Democratic Republic (1977-1988) (the other cells fail an earlier criterion). The 12 country-years of eligible codes are Germany 1977-1988, a composite with the GDR as one of its parts; this is why Western Europe starts in 1989 (NOTES items 17 and 23).
  • No two of the six groups, and no two NCD4 parts, share a code in any List (output/data_build/group_overlap.csv). The all-cause code of every List is the documented one in every cell (NOTES item 8).
  • Groups a List cannot separate are missing (Table 1.5). A group is also missing in a year when a required sub-item is not reported. A country-year with any needed group missing at 30-69 is not usable (‘group not isolable’: 1,232 country-years of all codes); 0 of the 935 ICD-7 country-years are usable.
  • COVID-19: Lists without a COVID-19 code end before 2020 and get 0; the Lists used from 2020 on (101, 103 and 104) all have one.
  • COPD (Result 3 only) is not required for a usable year but flagged (copd_ok): it can be separated in 4,583 of 5,125 usable country-years, and is missing in 151 country-years of the area windows, all in Latin America and the Caribbean (NOTES items 11-13 and 26).
  • Sub-groups are capped at their parent group (lung cancer at cancer, COPD at chronic respiratory diseases and NCD4 at all causes; IHD and stroke are scaled down together where their sum exceeds cardiovascular diseases), because unknown age is shared out within each group separately (NOTES item 27).

Coding changes

In plain words. When a country moves to another ICD revision or WHO list, a cause’s share of deaths can jump only because codes are grouped differently. For every such change, the last year of the old list was compared with the first year of the new one, and a relative change of more than 15% in a group’s share of deaths at 30-69 was flagged (for example, a share of 20% becoming more than 23% or less than 17%). The flags are warnings: no data were corrected, no year was excluded and the windows were not chosen to avoid them.

Exact rule.

  • 390 changes in 138 codes, 360 of them assessable at 30-69 (observed years only). Flagged, of the assessable changes: NCD4: 23 of 248 flagged, median change 2.1%; lung cancer: 81 of 309 flagged, median change 6.2%; COPD: 69 of 185 flagged, median change 10.4%; IHD: 74 of 264 flagged, median change 6.0%; diabetes: 151 of 356 flagged, median change 12.0%; chronic respiratory diseases: 101 of 244 flagged, median change 10.5%; stroke: 101 of 360 flagged, median change 6.6%; cancer: 53 of 360 flagged, median change 3.8%; cardiovascular diseases: 53 of 360 flagged, median change 3.5% (output/data_build/list_transitions.csv; NOTES item 15). 89 comparisons span more than one year, so they also contain the trend between the two years.
  • Inside the area windows there are 86 changes, at least one in each of the 53 countries; 43 of these 86 changes have no flag in any of the nine groups of Results 1-3. NCD4 is flagged at 1 of them: Sri Lanka 103 to 104, 2005-2006, +25% (output/data_build/window_transitions.csv; NOTES item 31; Section 7, ‘List changes’).
  • Two known steps were handled by the choice of codes in the dictionary instead (Causes above): ICD-7 cardiovascular diseases include cerebrovascular disease, and the former-Soviet COPD definition was checked at its List changes and kept as an approximation (NOTES item 12).

Not done. No bridge coding or comparability ratios were applied, flagged years were not excluded, and there is no run without them. The Study sub-project gives, for its country sets, the implied effect of each flagged change on an area’s deaths from each cause (lt_effect in Study/output/replication/probability.csv): at least 5% for 10 area-cause pairs, in Sub-Saharan Africa, Central Asia, South-eastern Asia, Southern Asia and Western Asia (Study NOTES item 7).

Ill-defined causes

In plain words. Some deaths are certified only with a symptom or as ‘cause unknown’: ICD-10 chapter R and the matching chapter of earlier revisions. These ill-defined deaths are a cause group of their own. They count in all causes, and so in the competing mortality (deaths from other causes) of Result 1, but never in cancer, cardiovascular diseases or NCD4. They were not redistributed, pro rata or by any other rule, in the data or in Results 1-3.

Why not. The analyses use deaths as certified, the method copied from Eu40_APC. Sharing them out pro rata would assume that ill-defined deaths have the same mix of causes as the certified deaths of the same area, sex, year and age, which the WHO files cannot confirm. Two steps deal with them instead: a year is not used when more than 20% of its deaths at 30-69 are ill-defined, and a sensitivity analysis measures what a redistribution would change (Table 1.6). Where the share is high, NCD4 rates are probably too low, since some ill-defined deaths are likely NCD4 deaths. Where the share changes, NCD4 trends are biased: a falling share (it fell most in Southern Asia and Latin America and the Caribbean) understates NCD4 declines, a rising share (it rose most in Western Europe and Western Asia) overstates them.

Does it matter? For trends, little in most areas: in the Study’s sensitivity analysis F8 (2000-2019, both sexes), redistribution moves the % change of the NCD4 probability by a median of 1.0 percentage points over the 13 areas, and by more than 5 points only in Southern Asia (-8.0% becomes -18.1%). For levels, the NCD4 probability in 2000 would be 0.3% (Australia and New Zealand) to 19.9% (Southern Asia) higher, and more than 5% higher in Southern Asia (19.9%), Sub-Saharan Africa (12.0%) and Latin America and the Caribbean (8.3%) (last column of Table 1.6). Results 1-3 were not re-run with redistributed deaths.

Exact rule.

  • Definition (ill_defined rows of the dictionary): ICD-7 780-795, ICD-8 780-796, ICD-9 780-799 and ICD-10 R00-R99. Other vague codes, such as heart failure or cancer of unspecified site, stay in their own groups.
  • Share of deaths at 30-69 over the windows: 0.5% (Australia and New Zealand) to 12.1% (Sub-Saharan Africa); first and last year of each window in Table 1.6.
  • Limit ill_max = 20% of deaths at 30-69, both sexes: 239 country-years are not usable for this reason (159 of eligible codes; most in Thailand 39, Honduras 16, Oman 16 and Dominican Republic 14). In 2 area countries the year just before the window fails the limit (Sri Lanka 1997, 20.2% and South Africa 1993, 20.4%); their usable runs, and so the windows of Southern Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa, start the year after.
  • In the area windows, ill-defined causes are above 5% of deaths at 30-69 in 411 of 2,133 country-years, above 10% in 94 and above 15% in 8 (highest Sri Lanka 1998, 18.8%).
  • Study sensitivity analysis F8: in each area, sex, year and age group at 30-69, each NCD4 cause is multiplied by (all - external - COVID-19) / (all - external - COVID-19 - ill-defined), which shares the ill-defined deaths out pro rata among all causes except external causes and COVID-19; years 2000-2019, both sexes, the Study’s country sets (as here except Western Asia: ARM ISR KWT and Eastern Europe: CZE HUN MDA POL ROU RUS SVK UKR; Table 1.6; Study NOTES item 1).
  • Module B (premature-death shares, Section 5.1) also writes a ‘redistributed’ variant to its CSV files: ill-defined deaths shared out in proportion to the other five groups. This raises every other share of a 5-year birth-cohort group by the same factor, 1 / (1 - ill-defined share): at 40-59 by a median of 1.6% and at most 14.0% (cohort groups observed at every age of the window). As the factor is the same for every cause, it cannot change the leading cause; the report shows the observed shares (and the variant without 2020-2022), not the redistributed ones.

Not done. The effect of a redistribution on Results 1-3 (cohort probabilities, crossing cohorts, lags) was not computed. No run with another ill-defined limit was made (04_area_series.R accepts ill_max= for such runs). Vague codes outside chapter R were not reassigned (Study NOTES item 1).

Gaps and interpolation

In plain words. Some countries skip one or a few years. Where 1-3 years in a row are missing inside a series, the deaths of every cause group, sex and age were filled with a straight line between the year before and the year after the gap; the WHO population was filled in the same way. Filled years count as usable and are marked (points in Figure D1). Longer gaps were not filled: they break a country’s series, and only its longest unbroken run is used.

Exact rule.

  • interp(): value = value before + (year - year before) / (year after - year before) x (value after - value before), on counts (deaths, person-years), not on rates; deaths and population are filled separately.
  • Deaths: 303 country-years in 87 codes, in runs of one year (100), two (73) and three (19); with the composite Germany 1979, which has a filled part, 304 (Data caveats). WHO population: 128 country-years at 30-69 (Table 1.1). Not filled: 54 gaps of 4 years or more (532 missing country-years in 45 codes).
  • In the area windows: 55 of 2,133 country-years in 15 countries, 1.4% of the person-years at 30-69. At least one country is filled in 43 of 513 area-years, and every country of the area in Central Asia 1983-1984 and Southern Asia 2008, 2016-2018.
  • A gap that spans a change of List spreads the coding step evenly over the filled years (List label ‘old/new’).
  • Known issue: the filling also applies to COVID-19. Puerto Rico 2018-2020 is filled between 2017 and 2021, so 1,093 COVID-19 deaths appear in 2018 and 2019, at most 0.023% of the deaths of Latin America and the Caribbean in a year (to be fixed at the next rebuild, NOTES item 92; Section 7). COVID-19 is not part of NCD4, so F1 and the NCD4 results are not affected; these deaths count only in all causes.

Not done. Gaps longer than 3 years were not filled, and no model-based or rate-based filling was used.

Peaks

In plain words. A peak in a series can be real (an epidemic, a crisis, a disaster) or come from the data (a change of cause list, a filled year, a step in the population). The build never removes, smooths or corrects a year because of a peak. It prevents some artefacts by design: each area keeps the same countries over its whole window, so countries entering or leaving cannot create a jump, and country-years that fail the usability rule are left out. It flags or records the rest: changes of cause list, filled and composite years, the source of the population and changes of territory.

For this section, every year-to-year change of at least 1 percentage point in F1 was listed: 85 of the 1,000 changes (13 areas, 2 sexes, every year of the windows), in 11 areas, most in Central Asia and Eastern Europe. In 6 areas one country holds more than 80% of the person-years (From countries to areas, below), so a peak of the area is a peak of that country. Table 1.7 groups the changes into episodes and traces each to the countries and causes behind it and to the build’s flags; the 23 isolated falls that belong to no episode are in its last row, checked against the flags but not traced one by one. The table also lists 3 one-year changes that do not show in F1 but do in other causes. In short, by verdict:

  • Real event (no artefact found, consistent with a known event; not checked against outside sources): Central Asia and Eastern Europe 1986-1994; Southern Asia 2005; Western Asia 1988; Western Asia 1993; Eastern Europe 1995-2006; Several areas 2020-2022.
  • Data artefact (the change comes from the data: a change of cause list, filled years, a step in the population, a shift between causes): Sub-Saharan Africa 1996; South-eastern Asia 2004-2005; Southern Asia 2006; Eastern Europe 1983-1984.
  • Mixed (partly an event, partly the data or the way deaths were certified): Sub-Saharan Africa 2010; Sub-Saharan Africa 2016-2019; Central Asia 2020-2022.
  • Not explained (no flag of the build explains it and no event was identified): Sub-Saharan Africa 1997-2015; Central Asia 1997-2005; South-eastern Asia 2001; Southern Asia 1999; Western Asia 1995-1996; Southern Europe 1969-1970.
  • Not traced: the 23 isolated falls of the last row.

Exact rule.

  • Same countries throughout: the number of countries summed is the same in every year of the window in 13 of the 13 areas (n_countries in data/derived/area_series.rds).
  • Change in F1 = 100 x (p in a year - p in the year before), for the period indicator by area and sex (output/sdg34/period.csv). A change belongs to the first row of Table 1.7 whose area and years contain it (‘Several areas’: every area); every change of at least 1 point is in the table, the isolated falls in its last row. Country values are at ages 30-69 inside the windows (data/derived/country_series.rds); changes of List come from output/data_build/window_transitions.csv.
  • Flags checked for a change from one year to the next, in every country of the area: a change of List, a filled or composite year, a change of population source. An isolated fall counts as a step in a decline when F1 in the next two years stays below its level before the fall; the country with the largest change is the one with the largest absolute change in NCD4 deaths at 30-69 (same sex).
  • No smoothing and no removal of outliers anywhere in the build; the only average is the 3-year mean WHO/WPP ratio of the population calibration (below). The models of Result 2 and Section 5 use 5-year cells, which average single-year peaks.

Not done. Steps inside WHO’s own population series (South Africa 2010), a shift between external and ill-defined causes (Russia 1983-1984) and COVID-19 deaths certified to other causes (Uzbekistan 2020-2022) are not checked by any rule of the build; they are reported here, not corrected. The isolated falls were not traced one by one, and no verdict was checked against outside sources.

Several areas 2020-2022 Rise in 2020 (males: Latin America and the Caribbean +0.60, Northern America +0.61 points), falls in 2022 Real event COVID-19 is 27.8% of deaths at 30-69 in Latin America and the Caribbean and 14.3% in Northern America in 2021; it counts in all causes, not in NCD4; NCD4 deaths rose too (Mexico’s NCD4 deaths at 30-69 +30.6% in 2020) Kept; COVID-19 is its own cause group
Isolated falls (8 areas) 1971-2018 23 falls of 1.04 to 1.93 points (21 males, 2 females) Not traced Males unless marked: Sub-Saharan Africa 1995 (females); Northern America 1975; Central Asia 2008, 2015, 2018; Southern Asia 2011; Western Asia 2001, 2005; Eastern Europe 2007, 2009, 2010, 2011, 2012, 2015, 2017; Northern Europe 1994; Australia and New Zealand 1971, 1975 (both sexes), 1986, 1990, 1993, 1995. In 21 of the 23, F1 stays below its level before the fall in the next two years (a step in a decline, not a one-year dip); not in Sub-Saharan Africa 1995 (females) and Central Asia 2018. In each, the NCD4 death rate at 30-69 falls in the country with the largest change in NCD4 deaths. 8 coincide with a change of List, a filled year or a change of population source in one of the area’s countries (Central Asia 2008; Western Asia 2001 and 2005; Eastern Europe 2007, 2012, 2015 and 2017; Northern Europe 1994) Kept; checked against the flags, not traced one by one

Population

In plain words. Rates need the population at risk. The WHO population supplied with the deaths was used wherever it exists, because it covers the same territory as the deaths. Outside Europe it often stops early, so the missing years and ages of a country-year with deaths were taken from the UN WPP, multiplied by the WHO/WPP ratio of the nearest WHO years (‘WPP calibrated’): this keeps the WHO level and territory. Countries without any WHO population take WPP as published.

Exact rule (details in ‘Population’ above and Table 1.1; NOTES item 84).

  • WHO population: 5,100 national country-years in 155 codes, ages harmonised as the deaths, unknown age dropped, gaps of 1-3 years filled.
  • WPP calibrated: ratio = WHO/WPP for that sex and age, the mean over up to 3 WHO years on each side, held constant beyond the first or last WHO year and interpolated between the two sides inside a longer WHO gap.
  • In the area windows the person-years at 30-69 are 70.3% WHO, 27.7% WPP calibrated and 2.0% WHO (interpolated); calibrated WPP enters 18 countries and uncalibrated WPP none.
  • The steps where a series switches between WHO and WPP (the seams) were measured (above), not smoothed.

Not done. No run with uncalibrated WPP. Steps inside WHO’s own population series are not checked (at 30-69, e.g. South Africa 2010 +9.5%, Armenia 2002 -16.9%, Moldova 2018 -23.8%). The WPP revision used is to be confirmed (NOTES item 84).

Code:

  • code/03_who_deaths.R: WHO population, ages harmonised, lines 170-173; UN WPP calibrated to WHO by sex and age, lines 178-189; population sources and seams, lines 207-219
  • Details: output/data_build/population_sources.csv, output/data_build/population_seams.csv

From countries to areas

In plain words. An area is a UN M49 sub-region. Inside it, each country contributes its longest unbroken run of usable years, if that run is at least 20 years long. Among all windows of at least 25 years, the window and the countries covering all of it with the most person-years at 30-69 were chosen, so that the same countries are summed in every year. Deaths and person-years of an area are plain sums over its countries, with no weighting. In 6 of the 13 areas one country holds more than 80% of the person-years at 30-69 in the window: Sub-Saharan Africa (South Africa, 96.9%), Northern America (United States of America, 89.8%), Central Asia (Uzbekistan, 83.1%), South-eastern Asia (Philippines, 94.1%), Southern Asia (Sri Lanka, 100.0%) and Australia and New Zealand (Australia, 83.5%); Southern Asia is Sri Lanka alone. In these areas a peak of the area series is a peak of that country.

Exact rule (details in ‘Usability rule’ and ‘Windows’ above, Tables 1.2-1.3, Figure D1).

  • Usability: the first failing criterion is recorded, in this order: population missing, group not isolable (a needed group cannot be separated), codes do not add up (Causes above), ill-defined above the limit (output/data_build/country_coverage.csv).
  • Longest run: interpolated and composite years count; ties go to the later run. Candidates: 96 eligible countries with a run of at least 20 years.
  • Window: at least 25 years (Southern Asia: 22, the longest run of its candidates); ties go to the longer, then the later window; the alternatives are kept in output/data_build/area_windows.csv.
  • Pooling: deaths and person-years summed by year, sex, age and cause group over the countries of the set; no standardisation or weighting at this step (data/derived/area_series.rds).

Not done. The choice of window does not look at the flags (changes of List, filled years); alternative windows are recorded, not used.

Code:

  • code/04_area_series.R: parameters ill_max, min_run, min_win, lines 22-24; usable country-years, first failing criterion, lines 50-59; candidates, lines 62-71; windows and country sets with the largest person-years, lines 73-95; area series = sums over the countries, lines 97-108
  • code/functions_pm.R: longest_run(), lines 61-66
  • Details: output/data_build/country_coverage.csv, output/data_build/areas_included.csv, output/data_build/area_windows.csv, data/derived/country_series.rds (R data, not in the repository), data/derived/area_series.rds (R data, not in the repository)

Where the details are

  • NOTES.md: items 1-3 (sources), 4-7 (countries, eligibility, composites), 8-15 (cause groups and changes of List), 16-19 (deaths and population), 20-25 (usability, runs, areas), 26-31 (COPD flag, sub-groups capped, territory changes, window alternatives, changes of List inside the windows), 84 (UN WPP), 85 (WHO data-quality assessment), 92 (known issues) and 107 (this section).
  • Study/NOTES.md: items 1 (ill-defined causes, F8), 4 (gaps) and 7 (changes of List).
  • Dictionaries (one row per column of each file): data/dict/dictionary.csv, data/derived/dictionary.csv and output/data_build/dictionary.csv; cause groups data/dict/who_cause_groups.csv; codes and eligibility data/dict/areas.csv.
